lessonTitle: The Red Eye and Sudden Visual Loss

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man tells you the vision in his left eye 'came down like a blind' while he was cleaning his teeth. It does not hurt and the eye looks perfectly normal. Meanwhile, down the corridor, a bright red, agonising eye is often less urgent than the quiet white one. Learning to tell them apart takes three questions and a torch.

blocks.markdown: **Red eye: sorting by danger.** A red eye is usually harmless. The task is to spot the few that threaten vision. Use the red flags: **reduced visual acuity, pain (as opposed to irritation), photophobia, an abnormal pupil, corneal clouding or an opacity, contact lens wear, trauma or a history of eye surgery**. Their absence supports a benign cause such as conjunctivitis; their presence needs same-day ophthalmology.

rows: Diffuse, greatest away from the cornea
Discharge: watery (viral), purulent (bacterial), itchy with allergy; often bilateral and spreading
Severe, with headache, nausea and vomiting
Mid-dilated, fixed, oval pupil; hazy (oedematous) cornea; firm globe
Older, hypermetropic, dim light or mydriatics as triggers
Ciliary flush: deeper red ring around the limbus
Small, irregular pupil (posterior synechiae); cells and flare in anterior chamber
Associations: HLA-B27 disease, IBD, sarcoid, JIA
White corneal infiltrate; uptake of fluorescein; dendritic pattern in herpes simplex
blocks.caption: Differentiating the common red eyes

blocks.title: Worked example: a red eye without red flags
blocks.prompt: A 24-year-old has had a gritty, red left eye with watery discharge for one day; the right eye became red this morning. Her flatmate had a cold. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye, pupils are normal and equal, the cornea is clear and there is no photophobia. Diagnose and advise.

steps.text: No red flags: vision is normal, no pain beyond grit, the pupils are normal, the cornea is clear and there is no photophobia.
Sequential bilateral redness with watery discharge after a cold fits viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis.

Advice: hygiene (separate towels, hand washing, avoid sharing), cool compresses and lubricants; it is self-limiting over one to two weeks and highly contagious; antibiotics are not usually needed (check local guidance).
Safety net: return urgently if pain, photophobia, reduced vision or contact lens wear develops.

blocks.answer: Viral conjunctivitis managed supportively with safety-netting for red flags.

blocks.title: Treatment principles
blocks.text: **Acute angle-closure glaucoma** is an emergency: lower the IOP with acetazolamide, topical agents (beta-blocker, alpha-agonist, then pilocarpine once pressure falls), analgesia and antiemetics, then definitive laser peripheral iridotomy. Do not use mydriatic drops. **Uveitis** needs topical corticosteroid and a cycloplegic under ophthalmology. **Bacterial keratitis** needs urgent scrapes and intensive topical antibiotics; topical steroids are not started before a diagnosis, and contact lenses are stopped. Check doses and routes against the BNF and local protocols.

blocks.markdown: **Painless sudden visual loss** is a distinct group. Think first of vascular and retinal causes: *central retinal artery occlusion* (profound loss within seconds, often embolic from carotid atheroma or the heart; a pale oedematous retina with a *cherry-red spot* at the fovea and a relative afferent pupillary defect); *central retinal vein occlusion* (blurred vision with widespread haemorrhages, a 'blood and thunder' fundus); *vitreous haemorrhage* (floaters, red haze, often diabetic); *retinal detachment* (flashes and floaters, then a curtain or shadow; urgent if the macula is still attached); *wet age-related macular degeneration* (distortion, central loss); *optic neuritis* (subacute, pain on movement, colour desaturation, young adults); and **giant cell arteritis** (age over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia, raised ESR or CRP) which causes anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy or retinal artery occlusion. *Amaurosis fugax*, transient monocular loss like a descending curtain that recovers in minutes, is a TIA of the retina and needs urgent vascular assessment.

blocks.title: Giant cell arteritis
blocks.text: If visual loss or jaw claudication accompanies a raised ESR or CRP in a patient over 50, start high-dose corticosteroid **immediately** without waiting for temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound, because the second eye can be lost within days. Doses and route (including IV methylprednisolone with visual loss) follow current BSR and local guidance. The ESR rises with age; a common convention for the upper limit is age/2 (men) or (age + 10)/2 (women), in mm/h, but a normal value does not exclude disease.

blocks.title: Worked example: sudden loss with a headache
blocks.prompt: A 76-year-old woman has had a week of headache with scalp tenderness and pain on chewing, then this morning lost vision in the left eye. Her ESR is 90 mm/h. Acuity is hand movements, left optic disc is pale and swollen. Explain what to do.

steps.text: Headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication in a person over 50 with a very high ESR and a swollen pale disc point to giant cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Age-adjusted ESR upper limit for a woman = (76 + 10)/2 = 43 mm/h, so 90 mm/h is clearly raised.
Start high-dose corticosteroid immediately in line with current guidance (route and dose per BSR/local), with gastric and bone protection; do not wait for biopsy.
Arrange same-day ophthalmology and rheumatology review, and temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound within the pathway; counsel about the risk to the other eye.

blocks.answer: Presumed giant cell arteritis: immediate steroids, same-day specialist review, confirm diagnosis afterwards.

blocks.markdown: **Examining the eye: a standard sequence.** (1) **Visual acuity**: each eye separately, with glasses or a pinhole, at 6 m on a Snellen chart (6/6 means the patient sees at 6 m what a normal eye sees at 6 m; 6/60 means seeing at 6 m what normal sees at 60 m). If the top letter cannot be seen, record counting fingers, hand movements, perception of light or no perception of light. (2) **Pupils**: size, shape, symmetry, direct and consensual reactions to light and near, and a *swinging torch test* for a **relative afferent pupillary defect** (RAPD): when the light swings to the affected eye, both pupils dilate, because the damaged optic nerve or retina signals less light than the healthy one. (3) Visual fields by confrontation, colour vision, eye movements. (4) The cornea with fluorescein, and IOP where trained. (5) **Fundoscopy**: check the red reflex, then the disc, vessels, macula and periphery; dilate with a short-acting mydriatic only when safe (never when angle closure is suspected, or when pupils must be monitored for neurological reasons).

blocks.caption: For Snellen acuity $6/d$ (metres); 6/6 gives 0, and each 0.1 logMAR is one line. Larger values mean worse acuity.

blocks.title: Recording acuity
blocks.text: State the chart, distance, and correction used (for example 'Snellen 6/12 with glasses, improving to 6/9 with pinhole'). An improvement with pinhole indicates a refractive error rather than disease. The usual UK driving standard is expressed on the Snellen scale (6/12), but the full rules are set by the DVLA, so check them.

points: A red eye with reduced vision, pain, photophobia, an abnormal pupil, a hazy cornea, contact lens wear or trauma needs same-day ophthalmology; conjunctivitis is the diagnosis only if these red flags are absent.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, firm eye), anterior uveitis (ciliary flush, small irregular pupil) and keratitis (corneal infiltrate) each have distinct signs and treatments.

Painless sudden visual loss includes retinal artery or vein occlusion, vitreous haemorrhage, detachment, optic neuropathy and giant cell arteritis; start steroids at once for suspected GCA with visual symptoms.
Examination: acuity (with pinhole), pupils with swinging torch test, fields, fundoscopy after safe dilatation; doses must be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old hypermetropic woman develops severe pain in her right eye and a headache while at the cinema, with nausea, vomiting and haloes around lights. The eye is red, the cornea is hazy, the right pupil is mid-dilated and does not react to light, and the globe feels firm. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Emergency ophthalmology referral with IOP-lowering treatment such as acetazolamide, then laser iridotomy
Topical antibiotics and review in a week
Mydriatic drops to allow a full fundus examination
Topical corticosteroid drops alone

questions.correctOptionText: Emergency ophthalmology referral with IOP-lowering treatment such as acetazolamide, then laser iridotomy

distractorRationale.c: Dilating the pupil can worsen angle closure.
distractorRationale.d: Not the treatment of angle closure.

questions.explanation: Severe pain, nausea, haloes, a hazy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a firm globe indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma, which can cause irreversible optic nerve damage within hours. IOP is lowered medically and the definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy; mydriatics are avoided.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis has a painful, photophobic red right eye. Visual acuity is mildly reduced. There is a ring of deep redness around the limbus, the pupil is small and irregular, and cells are seen in the anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anterior uveitis
Viral conjunctivitis
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
Subconjunctival haemorrhage

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ciliary flush, small irregular pupil and anterior chamber cells in a patient with HLA-B27-associated disease.
distractorRationale.b: Vision and pupils are normal in conjunctivitis.
distractorRationale.c: Typically a mid-dilated fixed pupil and hazy cornea.

questions.explanation: Ciliary flush, photophobia, a small irregular pupil from posterior synechiae and anterior chamber cells indicate anterior uveitis, associated with HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathy. Treatment is by ophthalmology with topical steroid and a cycloplegic.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman who sleeps in her contact lenses has a painful red left eye, photophobia and blurred vision. Fluorescein staining shows a corneal ulcer with a white infiltrate. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lens wear and refer urgently for corneal scrapes and intensive topical antibiotics
Prescribe topical corticosteroid drops and a pad
Reassure and advise lubricants
Continue wearing lenses with a new brand

questions.correctOptionText: Stop lens wear and refer urgently for corneal scrapes and intensive topical antibiotics

distractorRationale.b: Steroids before diagnosis can worsen infection and patching is avoided.

questions.explanation: A corneal infiltrate in a contact lens wearer is infective keratitis, often Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba, and risks perforation and scarring. She needs urgent ophthalmic assessment, scrapes for culture and intensive topical antibiotics, and steroids and patching are avoided at first.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden profound painless loss of vision in the right eye. The right pupil reacts poorly to direct light but consensually, there is a relative afferent pupillary defect, and the retina looks pale with a cherry-red spot at the macula. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergency assessment as for stroke, including ophthalmology and a search for an embolic source and GCA
Routine optician review
Topical steroid drops and review in a week
Reassure and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Emergency assessment as for stroke, including ophthalmology and a search for an embolic source and GCA
questions.explanation: A pale retina with a cherry-red macula and RAPD indicates central retinal artery occlusion, a stroke equivalent. He needs urgent vascular assessment for embolic sources and ESR and CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis, together with ophthalmic review.

questions.stem: In a patient over 50 with suspected giant cell arteritis and new visual loss, treatment with high-dose corticosteroids should be started immediately without waiting for a temporal artery biopsy.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Delay risks permanent blindness in the second eye, and biopsy remains diagnostic for some weeks after steroids are started. Dose and route follow current guidance, and specialist assessment is arranged urgently.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is investigated for suspected giant cell arteritis. Using the convention that the upper limit of normal ESR for women is (age + 10)/2 in mm/h, calculate her upper limit of normal ESR in mm/h.
questions.explanation: For a 68-year-old woman, (68 + 10)/2 = 39 mm/h. This is a convention-based guide and not a diagnostic threshold, and a normal ESR does not exclude giant cell arteritis.

questions.stem: A patient can read only the 6/36 line of the Snellen chart with the left eye. Using logMAR = log10(d/6) for acuity 6/d, calculate the logMAR value to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ratio d/6 = 36/6 = 6, and log10(6) = 0.778. Higher logMAR values indicate poorer acuity, and 6/6 corresponds to 0.

questions.stem: On the swinging torch test, when the light moves from the right eye to the left eye both pupils dilate, and when it moves back to the right eye both constrict. What does this show?

options.text: A relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye
A relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye
A third nerve palsy on the left
A normal response

questions.correctOptionText: A relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the left optic nerve or retina conducts less signal.
distractorRationale.b: Dilation would occur when the light moves to the right eye.
distractorRationale.c: Would give a dilated pupil with ptosis and eye movement deficits.
distractorRationale.d: Normal pupils constrict equally when the light swings to either eye.

questions.explanation: When the light is swung to an eye with reduced afferent input, the pupils paradoxically dilate because the brain senses less light than from the better eye. Here the dilation occurs when the light reaches the left eye, so the left eye has the defect.

questions.stem: List five causes of sudden painless visual loss in an older adult and, for each, state one distinguishing feature or the key urgent action.
markingGuide: Central retinal artery occlusion: profound loss, RAPD, cherry-red spot; stroke pathway
Central retinal vein occlusion: widespread haemorrhages ('blood and thunder'); ophthalmology
Giant cell arteritis: headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR/CRP; immediate steroids
Retinal detachment: flashes and floaters then curtain; urgent surgery
Vitreous haemorrhage: floaters, red haze, diabetic or tears; ophthalmology
Wet AMD: distortion with central loss; anti-VEGF; amaurosis fugax: TIA assessment
questions.explanation: A good answer links each cause to a key sign and recognises that several (artery occlusion, giant cell arteritis, detachment) are time-critical. Any five causes with correct features and actions earn full marks.

questions.stem: Describe a systematic examination of a patient with sudden loss of vision in one eye, including visual acuity, pupils and fundoscopy, and explain the precaution needed before dilating the pupils.
markingGuide: Visual acuity: each eye separately, with glasses or pinhole, Snellen at 6 m; counting fingers, hand movements, perception of light if needed
Pupils: size, shape, direct and consensual reactions; swinging torch test for RAPD
Visual fields by confrontation, colour vision, eye movements
Corneal examination with fluorescein; IOP if trained
Fundoscopy: red reflex, disc, vessels, macula, periphery
Dilate only if safe; avoid in suspected angle closure or when pupils must be monitored neurologically
questions.explanation: The marker expects the order acuity, pupils, fields, anterior segment and fundus, a correct description of RAPD and a statement of the precaution about mydriatics.
